newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: SOCCER-UNITED STATES FORCED TO RELIVE NIGHTMARE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UNITED STATES FORCED TO RELIVE NIGHTMARE.

text.p: The United States will be forced to relive a nightmare when they return to Costa Rica for a World Cup qualifying match on Sunday.

The North Americans claimed they were harassed and maltreated when they visited San Jose last year in a previous stage of the CONCACAF region qualifiers and they are concerned about a repeat performance on Sunday.
"We are worried. If there is any more violent action I can assure you that we will react vigorously," said Hank Steinbrecher, executive director of the United States soccer federation.
"I hope there will be enough security to protect our players."
Costa Rica is known as the Switzerland of Central America, thanks to its peaceful history and tradition of democracy. But the U.S. players left with a different impression.
Reports said that some were hit by batteries thrown from the crowd and that defender Paul Caligiuri was struck by a tear gas canister.
Goalkeeper Brad Friedel, who has played in front of volatile Turkish crowds, claimed he had never feared as much for his life as he did in San Jose.
To add insult to injury, the U.S. were outplayed on the pitch and lost 2-1, their first defeat in a World Cup qualifier since 1989.
Consequently their visit is of dual concern to their coach Steve Sampson.
"We are all worried about the return," he said. "We hope we can prove we can play better and that the security will be better."
The Costa Rican federation was subsequently fined $7,000 by FIFA, the international football federation, after the United States launched an official protest.
Costa Rican authorities have promised to step up security, mindful that they could lose home advantage if there are further incidents.

Costa Rica coach Horacio Cordero, however, who has already hit the headlines for banning his players from having sex until after the qualifiers are over, is furious that FIFA have appointed a Canadian official as their delegate at the game.
Canada are in the same six-team group and Cordero claims that an official from a non-participating country should have been chosen instead.
The United States have made a good start to the group, which is the final stage of the CONCACAF qualifying competition, beating Canada 3-0 at home and drawing 0-0 away to Jamaica.
Cordero, who took over in January, is considering changes to his attack after his team were held to a 0-0 draw at home by Mexico last Sunday.
Three teams qualify for France. Mexico and the U.S. are likely to take two places with Costa Rica, Canada, Jamaica and El Salvador scrapping for the third.
